newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germans finding unity is in eyes of beholder.
newsitem.headline: Germans finding unity is in eyes of beholder.

text.p: Six years after surmounting their Cold War-era division, Germans are finding that unity, like beauty, is in the eye of the beholder.
Western Germans, the richer majority in the reunited state, have forgotten their first flush of interest in the slightly exotic east. The "newcomers" are now taken for granted.
Feeling like wallflowers at a dance, "Ossis" (easterners) are shedding their fascination with everything western and speaking up more for themselves.
The result, on the sixth anniversary of their state merger on October 3, 1990, is a curious mix of two societies at the same time together and apart.

The Frankfurter Rundschau daily captured the mood on Wednesday in a cartoon showing an easterner and a westerner quietly sitting at a table eating a birthday cake. Beneath the table runs a deep abyss dividing the two.

"The reserves of east-west solidarity seem to have been exhausted," Reinhard Hoeppner, premier of the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, sighed in resignation recently. "These changes have worn us all out -- in the east as well as in the west."

The overall balance of six years of united Germany is positive. Bringing the eastern economy up to western standards is taking longer than expected, but few easterners would swap their new freedoms for a return to the communist past.
Although it still galls westerners to have to pay for the east, there has been no taxpayer revolt or political upheaval because of the new burdens the majority must bear.
An economic slowdown over the past year has slashed east German growth rates from a breathtaking nine to a modest three percent and brought public optimism tumbling down with it.

At a time when all of Germany must tighten its belt, the easterners -- only one-fifth of the total population -- see more clearly how little leeway they have with lower wages, weaker savings and shakier jobs than western workers.
More than ever, though, the mental differences between the two halves are upholding a kind of social division.

While westerners seem to have gone back to "business as usual", all but ignoring what happens across the vanished border, easterners "are demanding more independence and turning away from the west", the east Berlin weekly Wochenpost wrote.

In a poll on the trend known as "Eastern Spite", Wochenpost found that 90 percent of easterners said the region should take control of its destiny and 74 percent no longer wanted the western experts who came after 1990 to rebuild the economy.

"Things have definitely become more difficult between east and west," said Steffen Heitmann, justice minister in the eastern state of Saxony. "We know each other better and know how different we actually are."

"People don't want westerners telling them what to do any more," said Heitmann, adding that Ossis felt "swamped by foreigners" when they saw how many western experts had taken over key positions in the eastern economy and administration.
The western-dominated media hounded Heitmann in 1993 when he, during a short-lived bid for the German presidency, said Germany was being "swamped" by foreign asylum-seekers.
Another poll in Focus magazine showed wide differences in views -- 67 percent of easterners said state aid for the region was too low while only seven percent in the west agreed.
Seventy-two percent of the easterners said it would take more than 10 years before all Germans felt equal, while only 41 percent in the west thought the same.

Daniela Dahn, an east Berlin author who is a speaking tour star in the region but almost unknown in the west, says many easterners are disappointed that all the dreams they had at unification have not come true.
"Most people hoped that joining western society would bring a new kind of independence in all sorts of ways," she said.
Instead, many had to suddenly worry about jobs, debts, careers and other concerns hardly felt under communism.
"This disillusion has led many to resign themselves, but others have also developed this defiance that's now called Eastern Spite."
